questions.question: In a row of 40 students, Anil is 12th from the left and Sunil is 15th from the right. How many students are between them?
questions.solution: Sunil is 40 − 15 + 1 = 26th from the left. Students between = 26 − 12 − 1 = 13.

questions.question: Sanjay ranks 11th from the top and 29th from the bottom in a class. How many students are there in the class?
In a class of 35, Priya is 12th from the top and Neha is 9th from the bottom. How many students are between them?
questions.solution: Neha is 35 − 9 + 1 = 27th from the top. Between them: 27 − 12 − 1 = 14.

questions.question: In a certain code, each word is coded as the sum of the position values of its letters (A = 1, B = 2, … Z = 26). PEN is coded as 35. How is INK coded?
questions.solution: PEN = 16 + 5 + 14 = 35, which confirms the rule. INK = 9 + 14 + 11 = 34.

questions.question:
Statements: All engineers are graduates. Some graduates are managers.
Conclusions: I. Some engineers are managers II. Some managers are graduates
questions.solution: Converting 'some graduates are managers' gives some managers are graduates (II). The managers may not be engineers, so I does not follow.

questions.question:
Statements: No coder is a tester. All testers are analysts.
Conclusions: I. No coder is an analyst II. Some analysts are not coders
questions.solution: Testers are analysts and no tester is a coder, so some analysts (the testers) are not coders (II). Other analysts may be coders, so I does not follow.

questions.question: Six interns A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a row facing north. B sits at the left end. A sits two places to the right of B. C sits immediately to the right of A. D does not sit at the right end. E sits to the left of D. Who sits at the right end?
questions.solution: B is 1st, A is 3rd and C is 4th. The free seats are 2nd, 5th and 6th for D, E and F. D is not 6th and E is to the left of D, so D is 5th and E is 2nd. That leaves F in the 6th seat, at the right end.

questions.question: Five persons P, Q, R, S and T sit around a circular table facing the centre. P sits between Q and R. R sits immediately clockwise of P. S does not sit next to R. Who sits between T and Q?
questions.solution: Going clockwise from P: R is next, and Q is on P's other side, so Q is last. S and T take the two middle seats. S cannot be next to R, so S is the fourth seat and T the third. The order clockwise is P, R, T, S, Q. S sits between T and Q.

questions.question: A is the brother of B. B is the sister of C. D is the father of A. How is C related to D?
questions.solution: A, B and C are siblings, and D is the father of A, so D is the father of all three. C's gender is not given, so C is D's son or daughter.

questions.question: Pointing to a man, Sita says, 'He is the son of my mother's only brother.' How is the man related to Sita?
questions.solution: Sita's mother's only brother is her maternal uncle. His son is Sita's cousin.

questions.question: In a certain code, WORK is written as XQUO, where the letters are moved forward by 1, 2, 3 and 4 places respectively. How is PLAY written in that code?
questions.solution: P+1 = Q, L+2 = N, A+3 = D, Y+4 = C (after Z comes A, B, C). So PLAY is written QNDC.

questions.question: In a certain code, 'bright red car' is written as 'ka mi to', 'red car park' as 'mi to se' and 'park fast' as 'se ju'. How is 'bright' written in that code?
questions.solution: 'red car' is common to the first two statements and 'mi to' is common to the codes, so red and car are mi and to in some order. The remaining code in the first statement, 'ka', stands for bright.

questions.question: Find the next term: 7, 10, 16, 28, 52, ?
questions.solution: The differences are 3, 6, 12, 24, doubling each time, so the next difference is 48: 52 + 48 = 100.

questions.question: Find the next term: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ?
questions.solution: The terms are factorials: 1!, 2!, 3!, 4!, 5!. The next is 6! = 720.

questions.question: Find the next term: Z, X, U, Q, L, ?
questions.solution: The positions are 26, 24, 21, 17, 12. The differences are −2, −3, −4, −5, so the next is −6: 12 − 6 = 6, which is F.

questions.question: A man starts walking east, covers 10 m, turns right and walks 4 m, then turns right again and walks 10 m. How far and in which direction is he from the starting point?
questions.solution: East 10 m, then right (south) 4 m, then right (west) 10 m. The east and west moves cancel, so he is 4 m south of the start.

questions.question: Facing south-west, Anil turns 180° and then 90° anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
questions.solution: Turning 180° from south-west gives north-east. Turning 90° anticlockwise from north-east gives north-west.

questions.question: A clock gains 5 minutes every hour. It is set correctly at 6 AM. What time will it show when the true time is 2 PM?
questions.solution: From 6 AM to 2 PM is 8 hours. The clock gains 8 × 5 = 40 minutes, so it shows 2:40 PM.

questions.question: If 1 January 2026 is a Thursday, what day is 1 January 2027?
questions.solution: 2026 is not a leap year, so it has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day. The day moves forward by 1: Thursday → Friday.

questions.question: Which letter is the 5th to the left of the 20th letter from the left end of the alphabet?
questions.solution: The 20th letter is T. Five places to its left is the 15th letter, which is O.

questions.question: In a group of 45, Arun is 14th from the top and Bimal is 5 places below Arun. What is Bimal's position from the bottom?
questions.solution: Bimal is 14 + 5 = 19th from the top. From the bottom: 45 − 19 + 1 = 27th.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: Python, Java, Ruby, Excel, C++
questions.solution: Python, Java, Ruby and C++ are programming languages. Excel is a spreadsheet application.

questions.question: Five interns Ravi, Sita, Tarun, Uma and Vikas earn different stipends. Uma earns more than Ravi. Ravi earns more than Tarun. Sita earns less than Tarun. Vikas earns more than Uma. Who earns the least?
questions.solution: The clues give Vikas > Uma > Ravi > Tarun > Sita. Sita earns the least.

questions.question:
Statements: G > H ≥ I = J ≥ K
Conclusions: I. G > K II. K < H
questions.solution: G > H ≥ I = J ≥ K gives G > K (I follows). H ≥ K only, so K < H is not certain (II does not follow).

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 3, 10, 29, 65, 127
questions.solution: Each term should be a cube plus 2, that is n³ + 2: 1 + 2 = 3, 8 + 2 = 10, 27 + 2 = 29, 64 + 2 = 66, 125 + 2 = 127. The fourth term should be 66, so 65 is the odd one out.

questions.question: Five friends A, B, C, D and E have 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 marbles, one number each. A has 4 more marbles than C. B has more marbles than D but fewer than E. D has more marbles than C. Who has 6 marbles?
questions.solution: C has fewer marbles than D, and D < B < E, so C has fewer than three others. A = C + 4 is also more than C, so C has the fewest: 2. Then A = 6. D, B and E take 4, 8 and 10 in increasing order: D = 4, B = 8, E = 10. So A has 6 marbles.

questions.question: Which letter is the 9th to the left of the 6th letter from the right end of the English alphabet?
questions.solution: The 6th letter from the right is the (27 − 6) = 21st letter from the left, U. 9 places to its left is the 21 − 9 = 12th letter, L.

questions.question: If the first half of the English alphabet (A to M) is written in reverse order and the second half is left unchanged, which letter will be the 4th to the right of the 9th letter from the left?
questions.solution: The new sequence starts M L K J I H G F E D C B A N O P … The 9th letter from the left is E, and the 4th letter to its right is the 13th letter of the sequence, A.

questions.question: Which letter lies exactly midway between the 5th letter from the left and the 4th letter from the right of the English alphabet?
questions.solution: The 5th letter from the left is E (position 5) and the 4th from the right is W (position 27 − 4 = 23). The midpoint is position (5 + 23)/2 = 14, which is N.

questions.question: If every alternate letter of the English alphabet, starting with B, is removed, which letter will be the 7th from the right end of the remaining sequence?
questions.solution: Removing B, D, F, …, Z leaves A, C, E, …, Y — 13 letters. Counting from the right: Y, W, U, S, Q, O, M. The 7th is M.

questions.question: If the letters of the word FORMULATE are arranged in reverse alphabetical order (Z to A), which letter will be 3rd from the left?
questions.solution: In reverse alphabetical order the letters are U T R O M L F E A. The 3rd from the left is R.

questions.question: How many pairs of letters are there in the word FIGHTER that have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting in either direction)?
questions.solution: Check every pair against its alphabet gap. G–H are adjacent both in the word and in the alphabet. I (2nd) and E (6th) are 4 places apart in the word, and I(9) and E(5) are 4 apart in the alphabet. T (5th) and R (7th) are 2 places apart in the word, and T(20) and R(18) are 2 apart in the alphabet. No other pair matches, so there are 3 pairs.

questions.question: How many vowels are there in the English alphabet strictly between the 4th letter from the left and the 3rd letter from the right?
questions.solution: The 4th letter from the left is D and the 3rd from the right is X. The letters strictly between them run from E to W, which contain the vowels E, I, O and U — 4 vowels.

questions.question: If the English alphabet is written in reverse order (Z to A), which letter will be the 7th to the right of T?
questions.solution: In the reversed alphabet, moving right from T gives S, R, Q, P, O, N, M. The 7th letter is M.

questions.question: If the letters of the word PLANET are arranged in alphabetical order, how many letters will remain in the same position as in the original word?
questions.solution: Alphabetical order gives A E L N P T. Comparing with P L A N E T position by position, only N (4th) and T (6th) stay in place: 2 letters.

questions.question: Pointing to a girl, Arjun says, "She is the only daughter of my father's only son." How is the girl related to Arjun?
questions.solution: Arjun is a man, so his father's only son is Arjun himself. The girl is the only daughter of Arjun, i.e. his daughter.

questions.question: A is the mother of B. B is the sister of C. D is the son of C. E is the wife of D. How is E related to A?
questions.solution: B and C are A's children, so D (C's son) is A's grandson. E is the wife of A's grandson, so E is A's granddaughter-in-law.

questions.question: In a code, P × Q means P is the father of Q; P + Q means P is the brother of Q; P − Q means P is the sister of Q; P ÷ Q means P is the mother of Q. If A × B + C − D ÷ E, how is A related to E?
questions.solution: A × B: A is B's father. B + C and C − D: B, C and D are siblings, so A is also D's father. D ÷ E: D is E's mother. So A is the father of E's mother — E's grandfather.

questions.question: A family has six members P, Q, R, S, T and U, with two married couples. R is the wife of P. S is the only son of P and R. T is the sister of S and is unmarried. U is the daughter-in-law of R. Q is the son of U. How is T related to Q?
questions.solution: S is the only son of P and R, so U (R's daughter-in-law) is S's wife, and the two couples are P–R and S–U. Q, the son of U, is therefore S's son. T is S's sister, so T is Q's father's sister — Q's aunt.

questions.question: Introducing a man, Neha says, "His wife is the only daughter of my father." How is the man related to Neha?
questions.solution: Neha is a woman, so the only daughter of her father is Neha herself. The man's wife is Neha, so he is her husband.

questions.question: A is the brother of B. B is the son of C. D is the father of C. E is the daughter of D. How is A related to E?
questions.solution: A and B are C's children. C and E are both D's children, so E is C's sister. A is the son of E's sibling, so A is E's nephew.

questions.question: In a code, A @ B means A is the daughter of B; A $ B means A is the wife of B; A # B means A is the father of B; A & B means A is the brother of B. If P @ Q $ R # S & T, how is P related to T?
questions.solution: P @ Q: P is Q's daughter. Q $ R: Q is R's wife, so P is also R's daughter. R # S and S & T: S and T are R's children. P is a female child of the same parents as T, so P is T's sister (whatever T's gender).

questions.question: Pointing to a woman, Kunal says, "She is the mother of the only grandson of my mother's husband." Kunal has no brothers or sisters. How is the woman related to Kunal?
questions.solution: Kunal's mother's husband is Kunal's father. As Kunal has no siblings, any grandson of his father must be Kunal's son. The mother of Kunal's son is Kunal's wife.

questions.question: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 8:25?
How many times do the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock coincide between 3 p.m. and 9 p.m.?
questions.solution: The hands coincide every 720/11 = 65 5/11 minutes, i.e. at 720k/11 minutes after 12 o'clock (k = 0, 1, 2, …). Between 3 p.m. (180 minutes) and 9 p.m. (540 minutes) this needs 180 < 720k/11 < 540, i.e. 2.75 < k < 8.25, so k = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8: 6 times (about 3:16, 4:22, 5:27, 6:33, 7:38 and 8:44). The 9 o'clock coincidence comes only at about 9:49.

questions.question: At what time between 2 o'clock and 3 o'clock will the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock point in exactly opposite directions?
questions.solution: At 2:00 the minute hand is 60° behind the hour hand. It gains 5.5° per minute and must get 180° ahead, a total gain of 60 + 180 = 240°. Time = 240/5.5 = 480/11 = 43 7/11 minutes past 2.

questions.question: A clock loses 4 minutes every hour. It is set right at 8 a.m. What is the correct time when this clock shows 8 p.m. the same day?
questions.solution: In 60 minutes of correct time the clock shows only 56 minutes. When it shows 12 hours = 720 minutes, the correct time elapsed is 720 × 60/56 = 771 3/7 minutes = 12 hours 51 3/7 minutes. So the correct time is 8:51 3/7 p.m.

questions.question: On which day of the week did 26 January 1950 fall?
questions.solution: Odd days up to 31 December 1949: 1600 years give 0, the next 300 years give 1, and 49 years (12 leap + 37 ordinary) give 12 × 2 + 37 = 61, i.e. 5. Total so far 0 + 1 + 5 = 6. Add 26 days of January: 6 + 26 = 32, and 32 leaves remainder 4 on division by 7. Day 4 (counting Sunday as 0) is Thursday.

questions.question: 3 March 2027 is a Wednesday. What day of the week will 3 March 2028 be?
questions.solution: The period from 3 March 2027 to 3 March 2028 includes 29 February 2028 (2028 is a leap year), so it has 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 days. 2 days after Wednesday is Friday.

questions.question: The calendar of 2026 will be repeated exactly (same days on the same dates) in which of these years?
questions.solution: 2026 is an ordinary year. Counting odd days from 2026: 2026 (1), 2027 (1), 2028 (2), 2029 (1), 2030 (1), 2031 (1), 2032 (2), 2033 (1), 2034 (1), 2035 (1), 2036 (2) — a total of 14, a multiple of 7. So 2037 starts on the same day as 2026, and it is also an ordinary year, so its calendar is identical. (2032 and 2036 are leap years, and 2034 starts on a different day.)

questions.question: In a certain code, MOTHER is written as SFIUPN. How is FATHER written in that code?
questions.solution: The word is reversed and each letter is then moved one place forward: MOTHER → REHTOM → SFIUPN. Similarly FATHER → REHTAF → SFIUBG.

questions.question: In a certain code, ROAD is written as 9-12-26-23. How is LANE written in that code?
questions.solution: Each letter is replaced by its position counted from the end of the alphabet (Z = 1, …, A = 26): R = 9, O = 12, A = 26, D = 23. So L = 15, A = 26, N = 13, E = 22, giving 15-26-13-22.

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'come and go' is written as 'pa ri sa', 'go and run' as 'ri na pa', and 'run fast now' as 'ta na ke'. What is the code for 'come'?
questions.solution: 'and go' is common to the first two sentences, and 'pa ri' is common to their codes, so 'and' and 'go' are coded as 'pa' and 'ri' in some order. The remaining word of the first sentence, 'come', must be 'sa'.

questions.question: If PAINT is coded as 74128 and EXCEL as 93596, how is ACCEPT coded?
questions.solution: Each letter has a fixed digit: P = 7, A = 4, I = 1, N = 2, T = 8 and E = 9, X = 3, C = 5, L = 6 (E = 9 is consistent at both ends of EXCEL). So A C C E P T = 4 5 5 9 7 8 = 455978.

questions.question: In a certain code, PLANET is written as QKBMFS. How is CORNER written in that code?
questions.solution: Letters in odd positions move one step forward and letters in even positions move one step back: P+1 = Q, L−1 = K, A+1 = B, N−1 = M, E+1 = F, T−1 = S. So C+1 = D, O−1 = N, R+1 = S, N−1 = M, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q: DNSMFQ.

questions.question: In a certain code, BAD = 8 and CAB = 6. Following the same rule, what is the code for DEED?
questions.solution: The code is the product of the alphabet positions: BAD = 2 × 1 × 4 = 8 and CAB = 3 × 1 × 2 = 6. So DEED = 4 × 5 × 5 × 4 = 400.

questions.question: In a certain code, ROSE is written as SQVI. How is LILY written in that code?
questions.solution: The letters move forward by 1, 2, 3 and 4 places in turn: R+1 = S, O+2 = Q, S+3 = V, E+4 = I. So L+1 = M, I+2 = K, L+3 = O and Y+4 = C (counting past Z back to A, B, C): MKOC.

questions.question: Kiran walks 6 km east, turns left and walks 8 km, then turns left again and walks 12 km. How far and in which direction is she from her starting point?
questions.solution: Take the start as (0, 0). After 6 km east she is at (6, 0); turning left she faces north and reaches (6, 8); turning left again she faces west and reaches (6 − 12, 8) = (−6, 8). Distance = √(6² + 8²) = 10 km, towards the north-west.

questions.question: A man is facing east. He turns 45° clockwise, then 180° anticlockwise, and then 90° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
questions.solution: Measure bearings clockwise from north: east = 90°. After the turns: 90 + 45 = 135°, then 135 − 180 = −45° (i.e. 315°), then 315 + 90 = 405° = 45°, which is north-east.

questions.question: Point A is 9 m west of point B. Point C is 12 m south of point B. How far is C from A, and in which direction is C with respect to A?
questions.solution: Take B = (0, 0): A = (−9, 0) and C = (0, −12). From A, C is 9 m to the east and 12 m to the south, so AC = √(9² + 12²) = 15 m and C is to the south-east of A.

questions.question: At 4 p.m. on a sunny day, Rina stands facing her own shadow. Which direction is she facing?
questions.solution: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so shadows fall towards the east. Facing her shadow, Rina faces east.

questions.question: Rahul leaves his house and walks 4 km north. He turns right and walks 6 km, turns right and walks 9 km, turns left and walks 6 km, and finally turns left and walks 5 km. How far and in which direction is he from his house?
questions.solution: Take the house as (0, 0). North 4 → (0, 4); right (east) 6 → (6, 4); right (south) 9 → (6, −5); left (east) 6 → (12, −5); left (north) 5 → (12, 0). He is 12 km due east of his house.

questions.question: P and Q start from the same point. P walks 7 km north and then 3 km east. Q walks 3 km west and then 1 km south. What is the straight-line distance between P and Q now?
questions.solution: With the start at (0, 0), P is at (3, 7) and Q at (−3, −1). The horizontal gap is 3 + 3 = 6 km and the vertical gap 7 + 1 = 8 km, so PQ = √(6² + 8²) = 10 km.

questions.question: A wall clock is fixed so that its 12 points towards the north-east. In which direction will the hour hand point at 1:30?
questions.solution: At 1:30 the hour hand is 1.5 × 30 = 45° clockwise from the 12. The 12 points north-east (45° from north), so the hour hand points at 45 + 45 = 90° from north, which is east.

questions.question: Village Q is 10 km north of village P. Village R is 6 km east of Q. Village S is 2 km south of R, and village T is 6 km west of S. Where is T with respect to P?
questions.solution: Take P = (0, 0). Then Q = (0, 10), R = (6, 10), S = (6, 8) and T = (0, 8). T is 8 km due north of P.

questions.question:
Statements: M > N ≥ O = P, Q < O
Conclusions: I. M > P II. Q < N
questions.solution: Combining: M > N ≥ O = P gives M > P, so I follows. Q < O = P and O ≤ N gives Q < N, so II follows. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: A ≥ B = C, D ≤ C
Conclusions: I. A ≥ D II. D > B
questions.solution: A ≥ B = C ≥ D gives A ≥ D, so I follows. Since D ≤ C = B, D can never be greater than B, so II does not follow. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: R ≥ S > T, U ≥ S
Conclusions: I. R > U II. U ≥ T
questions.solution: R and U are both at least S, but nothing links R with U directly, so I does not follow. U ≥ S > T gives U > T, which makes U ≥ T true, so II follows. Only II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: K ≤ L = M, M ≥ N
Conclusions: I. K < M II. K = M
questions.solution: K ≤ L = M gives K ≤ M. Neither K < M nor K = M is certain on its own, but one of them must be true and they cover every case of K ≤ M. So either I or II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: W > X < Y ≥ Z
Conclusions: I. W > Z II. Y > W
questions.solution: W and Y are both greater than X but are not compared with each other, and Z is linked only through Y. So neither W > Z nor Y > W can be established. Neither follows.

questions.question:
Statements: P < Q ≥ R = S, T ≥ S
Conclusions: I. T > R II. T = R
questions.solution: T ≥ S = R gives T ≥ R. Neither T > R nor T = R is certain, but together they cover every possibility, so either I or II follows.

questions.question:
In a certain code, 'P # Q' means P is not smaller than Q; 'P @ Q' means P is neither greater nor smaller than Q; 'P % Q' means P is greater than Q; and 'P & Q' means P is smaller than Q.
Statements: A # B, B @ C, C % D
Conclusions: I. A % D II. B # D
questions.solution: Decoding: A ≥ B, B = C, C > D, i.e. A ≥ B = C > D. So A > D, which is A % D (I follows), and B > D, which makes 'B is not smaller than D' (B # D) true (II follows). Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: X ≤ Y < Z, W > Z
Conclusions: I. W > X II. Y ≥ W
questions.solution: W > Z > Y ≥ X gives W > X, so I follows. The same chain gives W > Y, so Y ≥ W is false. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: J > K ≥ L, M ≤ L, N > M
Conclusions: I. N > K II. J > M
questions.solution: N is greater than M only; it is not compared with K, so I does not follow. J > K ≥ L ≥ M gives J > M, so II follows. Only II follows.

questions.question: Find the next term: 4, 10, 28, 82, 244, ?
questions.solution: Each term is 3 times the previous term minus 2: 4 × 3 − 2 = 10, 10 × 3 − 2 = 28, 28 × 3 − 2 = 82, 82 × 3 − 2 = 244, so the next is 244 × 3 − 2 = 730.

questions.question: Find the wrong number in the series: 2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 96, 191
questions.solution: Each term should be 2 × (previous) + 1: 2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, 191. The term 96 should be 95 (and 2 × 95 + 1 = 191 confirms it), so 96 is wrong.

questions.question: Find the next term: BDF, HJL, NPR, ?
questions.solution: The letters run B, D, F, H, J, L, N, P, R, … skipping one letter each time, taken three at a time. The next group is T, V, X.

questions.question: Find the next term: 1, 4, 27, 256, ?
questions.solution: The terms are 1¹, 2², 3³, 4⁴, so the next term is 5⁵ = 3125.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 13, 17, 19, 27, 29
questions.solution: 13, 17, 19 and 29 are prime numbers. 27 = 3 × 9 is not prime, so it is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 216, 343, 512, 720, 1000
questions.solution: 216 = 6³, 343 = 7³, 512 = 8³ and 1000 = 10³ are perfect cubes. 720 is not a perfect cube (9³ = 729).

questions.question: Find the odd one out: Lion, Tiger, Leopard, Wolf, Cheetah
questions.solution: Lion, tiger, leopard and cheetah are all big cats (cat family). The wolf belongs to the dog family, so it is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: BCD, FGH, JKM, PQR
questions.solution: BCD, FGH and PQR are three consecutive letters of the alphabet. In JKM, L is skipped between K and M, so JKM is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 35, 48, 63, 80, 100
questions.solution: 35 = 6² − 1, 48 = 7² − 1, 63 = 8² − 1 and 80 = 9² − 1. The pattern continues with 10² − 1 = 99, so 100 does not fit.

questions.question: Find the odd pair: 3 : 27, 4 : 64, 5 : 125, 6 : 216, 7 : 350
questions.solution: In each pair the second number is the cube of the first: 3³ = 27, 4³ = 64, 5³ = 125, 6³ = 216. But 7³ = 343, not 350, so 7 : 350 is the odd pair.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: Rupee, Dollar, Yen, Euro, Kilogram
questions.solution: Rupee, dollar, yen and euro are currencies. Kilogram is a unit of mass, so it is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: ACE, IKM, OQS, UWY, EGJ
questions.solution: In ACE, IKM, OQS and UWY each letter is 2 places after the previous one (A+2 = C, C+2 = E). In EGJ, G+2 would be I, not J, so EGJ is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 121, 242, 363, 484, 595
questions.solution: 121, 242, 363 and 484 are 121 × 1, 121 × 2, 121 × 3 and 121 × 4. The next multiple would be 121 × 5 = 605; 595 is not a multiple of 121 (or even of 11), so it is the odd one out.

questions.question: Find the odd one out: 123, 234, 345, 456, 568
questions.solution: 123, 234, 345 and 456 are made of three consecutive digits in increasing order. In 568 the digit 7 is skipped, so it is the odd one out.

questions.question:

questions.question:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on different floors of a 7-storey building (ground floor = floor 1, top floor = floor 7). K lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 4. Exactly two persons live between K and N. L lives immediately below N. O lives below M, and M lives below J. P lives immediately above J, on an even-numbered floor.
Who lives on floor 5?
questions.solution: Brute-force over all orders leaves one arrangement (floor 1 to 7): O, M, L, N, J, P, K. If K were on floor 5, N would be on floor 2 and L on floor 1, leaving no room for O < M < J with P immediately above J on an even floor. So K is on floor 7, N on 4, L on 3; P must be on 6 with J on 5, and O, M take floors 1 and 2. Floor 5 is J.

Which lecture is held on Thursday?

questions.question:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F have different heights. C is taller than only two of them. E is taller than A, and A is taller than C. F is shorter than D. B is not the shortest. E is not the tallest. D is taller than B.
Who is the tallest?
questions.solution: The unique order from tallest to shortest is D, E, A, C, B, F. C is 4th tallest, so B and F are the two below C. E and A are above C; D is taller than both B and F, so D cannot be among the two below C, and D, E, A fill the top three; E is not the tallest and A is below E, so D is tallest, then E, then A. B is not the shortest, so B is 5th and F 6th.

questions.solution: Bina's position from the front is N − 8 + 1 = N − 7. questions.solution: The locks that are doors cannot be windows, because no door is a window, so some locks are not windows: I follows. Keys are not linked to windows by any statement, so II is not certain. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: Some rivers are lakes. All lakes are ponds. No pond is a well.
Conclusions: I. Some rivers are not wells. II. Some lakes are wells.
questions.solution: The rivers that are lakes are also ponds, and no pond is a well, so those rivers are not wells: I follows. Every lake is a pond and no pond is a well, so no lake is a well: II is false. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: Some pens are markers. Some markers are not crayons. All crayons are pens.
Conclusions: I. Some markers are crayons. II. Some pens are crayons.
questions.solution: Nothing forces any marker to be a crayon (the markers may lie wholly outside crayons), so I does not follow. Crayons exist and every crayon is a pen, so some pens are crayons: II follows. Only II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few birds are eagles. All eagles are hunters.
Conclusions: I. Some birds are hunters. II. All birds are hunters.
questions.solution: 'Only a few birds are eagles' means some birds are eagles and some birds are not. The birds that are eagles are hunters, so some birds are hunters: I follows. The birds that are not eagles may or may not be hunters, so II is not certain. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: All fans are coolers. Some coolers are heaters. No heater is a light.
Conclusions: I. Some fans being heaters is a possibility. II. All lights being fans is a possibility.
questions.solution: Fans and heaters can overlap inside coolers, so I is possible. Lights only have to stay away from heaters; they can all sit inside the part of fans that is not heaters, so II is also possible. Both follow.

questions.question: Who sits directly opposite F?
questions.solution: Fix A. F is on A's immediate left and D is second to A's right. C, H and B sit together in that order going left (B is second to the left of C, with H between them). The free seats are the second, third, fourth, fifth and seventh to the left of A (D holds the sixth). If C, H and B take the third, fourth and fifth seats, G must sit opposite H, which is A's seat, so that fails. So C, H and B take the second, third and fourth seats to the left of A, G is opposite H in the seventh seat, and E takes the fifth. Going left (clockwise) from A: A, F, C, H, B, E, D, G. F and E are 4 seats apart, so E is opposite F.

questions.solution: R takes the first seat from the left, so P takes the third. questions.question: A stationery shop sold 240 items last week, made up only of pens, pencils and erasers. Pens made up 40% of the items sold, and 30 more pencils than erasers were sold. One-third of the pencils and one-third of the erasers were sold at a discount. How many pencils and erasers in total were sold at a discount?
questions.solution: Pens = 40% of 240 = 96, so pencils + erasers = 240 − 96 = 144. With pencils = erasers + 30: 2 × erasers = 114, so erasers = 57 and pencils = 87. Sold at a discount: 87 ÷ 3 + 57 ÷ 3 = 29 + 19 = 48.

questions.solution: Number of matches = 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28. Every match hands out exactly 2 points in total (2 + 0 for a result, 1 + 1 for a draw), so the total is 28 × 2 = 56, whatever the results.

questions.question: A town's streets form a square grid. To go from junction A to junction B a cyclist must travel 4 blocks east and 3 blocks north, moving only east or north at each junction. Junction C lies 2 blocks east and 1 block north of A. How many of these shortest routes from A to B pass through C?
questions.solution: A to C needs 2 east and 1 north moves in some order: 3!/(2! × 1!) = 3 ways. C to B needs the remaining 2 east and 2 north: 4!/(2! × 2!) = 6 ways. Routes through C = 3 × 6 = 18.
